title: Habits on Purpose
author: Kristi Angevine, MD
description: A podcast created to empower high-achieving women to develop intentional habits and build fulfilling lives. Host Dr. Kristi Angevine, an OB/Gyn turned Certified Life Coach, shares practical strategies to move beyond perfectionism, overwhelm, and guilt.

episodes.title: 241: The Power of Tapping Into Your Body with Dr. Amruti Choudhry
episodes.summary: Dr. Amruti Choudhry talks about coaching clients to notice body signals, slow down, and build emotional awareness, with practical advice for busy professionals who live mostly in their heads.

episodes.title: 240: How to Engage with Your Inner Critic
episodes.summary: Kristi offers a different approach to self-critical thoughts: engaging them in dialogue instead of resisting them, and how that shift changes daily stress and self-judgment.

episodes.title: 239: Self-Doubt, Perfectionism & Finding Your Purpose with Dr. Devon Gimbel
episodes.summary: Dr. Devon Gimbel shares how she built a travel rewards business while working through perfectionism and self-doubt, including identifying core values and acting despite internal resistance.

episodes.title: 238: 'I Should Know Better' and 'I Should Be Further Along'
episodes.summary: Two draining thought patterns that create recurring stress, and proactive strategies for handling the beliefs that undermine progress and self-trust.

episodes.title: 237: How to Change Your Relationship with Rest
episodes.summary: Why rest, leisure, and play feel hard to access even when you want them, why disengaging from productivity is so uncomfortable, and how to reframe rest as essential rather than indulgent.

episodes.title: 236: The Problem with Self-Judgment (& What to Replace It With)
episodes.summary: How self-judgment operates quietly and unproductively, why it doesn't improve performance, and an antidote for daily self-critical patterns.

articles.question: Why is it so hard for me to rest?
articles.metaDescription: Dr. Kristi Angevine of Habits on Purpose on why rest feels hard for high achievers, the hidden rules that block it, and a two-week reset.
articles.intro: Rest is hard for you because somewhere along the way you picked up rules about when it's allowed, and most of those rules say "not yet." That's the core of what Dr. Kristi Angevine, physician turned life coach and host of Habits on Purpose, explains in this episode. You were born knowing how to rest and play. The skill isn't gone. It's buried under overcommitment, perfectionism, and a belief that worth comes from output.

sections.heading: What counts as rest (and what doesn't)
sections.body:
Kristi starts with a definition, because a lot of what we call rest isn't. Scrolling while thinking about tomorrow's to-do list isn't rest. Neither is a hobby you've turned into a side hustle with metrics.

Her definition is simple: rest is anything done without an agenda, without a box to check, without a task to complete. Leisure and play fall under the same umbrella. The moment there's a goal attached, it stops being rest and becomes another job.

She also points out that these are things we're born knowing how to do. Watch a small child and you'll see it. What changed isn't your ability. It's the set of beliefs you've layered on top of it.

quote.text: Rest is anything that's done without an agenda, to check off a box, or complete a task.
quote.speaker: Kristi Angevine

sections.heading: Overextension and perfectionism eat the time first
sections.body:
The most obvious reason rest doesn't happen is that there's no room for it. Kristi describes being overextended as having more things you want to do than you actually have time for. If your commitments already exceed your hours, rest is always the thing that gets cut.

Perfectionism makes this worse in a sneaky way. Tasks that could take 30 minutes take two hours because "done" isn't good enough. That extra time comes from somewhere, and it usually comes from the space where rest would have been.

Her suggestion is to audit honestly. Look at what's on your plate versus what fits, and notice where a perfectionist standard is quietly inflating the time cost of ordinary tasks.

quote.text: Perfectionism may contribute to you feeling overextended.
quote.speaker: Kristi Angevine

sections.heading: The hidden rules: only when sick, only after success
sections.body:
This is the part of the episode that tends to land hardest. Kristi walks through the unspoken rules many high achievers carry about when rest is permitted.

One rule says rest is only allowed in the setting of illness or injury. You can lie down if you have a fever. Otherwise, get up. Another says rest is only allowed after success, once the project ships or the list is empty, which for most of us means never.

Underneath both is a belief she names directly: the more I do, the more worthy I am. If that's running in the background, rest will always feel like a small failure. She also flags the guilt rule, the idea that when you rest you're dumping on your partner or burdening your kids, and invites you to check whether that's actually true or just a story that keeps you moving.

quote.text: The more that I do, the more worthy I am.
quote.speaker: Kristi Angevine

sections.heading: The heart doesn't skip diastole
sections.body:
As a physician, Kristi reaches for a physiology metaphor that reframes the whole thing. The heart works in two phases: systole, when it contracts, and diastole, when it relaxes and fills. Diastole isn't the lazy phase. It's when the heart fills with the blood it's about to pump.

Skip the rest between contractions and the heart can't fill. Skip your rest and you can't either. Rest isn't the reward for working. It's the phase that makes the next effort possible.

Her practical experiment is small. For two weeks, take five to ten minutes a day and do nothing. No phone, no plan. Then watch what your mind does. The thoughts that show up in those minutes are the rules that have been blocking your rest all along, and once you can see them, you can start to rewrite them.

quote.text: Without adequate resting between contractions, adequate filling cannot occur.
quote.speaker: Kristi Angevine

keyTakeaways: Rest is anything done without an agenda; if there's a goal attached, it's not rest.
Overcommitment and perfectionism quietly consume the time where rest would have gone.
Most people carry hidden rules like "rest only when sick" or "rest only after success."
The belief that doing more makes you more worthy is what makes rest feel like failure.
Try five to ten minutes of doing nothing every day for two weeks and observe the thoughts that surface.

faq.q: Is it normal to feel guilty when resting?
faq.a: Kristi says it's common, especially for high achievers, and usually comes from a belief that rest burdens others or that worth depends on output. The guilt is a signal to examine the belief, not proof that rest is wrong.

faq.q: How much rest do I actually need?
faq.a: The episode doesn't prescribe a number. It focuses on making rest a regular phase, like the heart's filling phase, rather than something earned. Her starting experiment is five to ten minutes a day.

faq.q: Does watching TV count as rest?
faq.a: By her definition, only if it's done without an agenda. If you're using it to avoid something or mentally running your list the whole time, it's not doing the job rest is supposed to do.
